headline: Sermorelin’s
missing approval.
dek: It was FDA approved as Geref. Both approvals were withdrawn in 2009.
photoAlt: An older man in a cardigan holds a sleep study report.
byline: Adonis Men’s Health · Checked Oct 31, 2026 · Clinical review pending

glance.label: Sleep trials
glance.line: No sermorelin trial with sleep as its result. Magnesium: low-certainty evidence.

glance.label: Banned in sport
glance.line: Sermorelin, CJC-1295, ipamorelin and the GHRPs are banned at all times.

body: Men who sleep badly are offered a long list of fixes, and the most heavily marketed ones work through growth hormone. The idea is that the body releases much of its growth hormone during deep sleep, so a drug that raises it might deepen sleep too. The best known of these drugs, [[/sermorelin|sermorelin]], has an unusual history: it was once FDA approved, and it is not anymore.

Sermorelin is a short version of growth hormone-releasing hormone, the signal that tells the pituitary gland to release growth hormone. FDA approved it as Geref, first in 1990 as a test of whether the pituitary can release growth hormone, and in 1997 to treat children with growth hormone deficiency.[^geref1][^geref2] Then its maker stopped selling it. A 2009 Federal Register notice listed Geref among products whose holders “notified the agency in writing that the drug products were no longer marketed and requested that the approval of the applications be withdrawn.”[^fr2009] The withdrawal took effect on June 18, 2009.[^fr2009]

The reason was not safety. In 2013, FDA published its finding that Geref was “not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness,”[^fr2013] a step that leaves room for generic versions. But no sermorelin product is FDA approved today. So when a product is described as FDA approved, it is pointing to an approval that ended in 2009. Compounded sermorelin is not FDA approved, and using it for sleep is off-label. In 2022, a compounding pharmacy recalled lots of several injectable products, including sermorelin, because “these compounded products were found to be out-of-specification.”[^olympia]

The sleep research behind sermorelin is indirect. We found no trial of sermorelin with sleep as its main result. In a 1999 German study, 12 young and 11 older healthy men were given growth hormone-releasing hormone or a placebo by nasal spray before bed.[^perras] The authors reported that the hormone “increased rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep and slow wave sleep (SWS), with this influence concentrating on the second half of sleep time.”[^perras] The abstract does not say whether the hormone used was sermorelin.

A group of related peptides is sold for the same purpose, with less behind them. [[/cjc-1295|CJC-1295]] is a longer-acting relative of sermorelin, and [[/ipamorelin|ipamorelin]], [[/ghrp-2|GHRP-2]], [[/ghrp-6|GHRP-6]] and [[/hexarelin|hexarelin]] push the pituitary to release growth hormone by another route. FDA placed ipamorelin acetate in its category of compounding substances that may present significant safety risks in 2023, noting that “a study published in literature identified serious adverse events including death when ipamorelin was administered intravenously for improving gastric motility.”[^cat2] For GHRP-6, FDA writes that “the available data reveal safety concerns including potential effect on cortisol and increase in blood glucose due to decreases in insulin sensitivity.”[^cat2] For CJC-1295, it says it “has identified serious adverse events associated with CJC-1295 including increased heart rate and systemic vasodilatory reaction.”[^cat2] The pill [[/ibutamoren|ibutamoren]], sold as MK-677, is on the same list. FDA says it “poses significant safety risks due to the potential for congestive heart failure in certain patients,”[^cat2] and cites a hip-fracture trial that “was terminated early due to a potential safety signal of congestive heart failure.”[^cat2]

One peptide in this family is approved, but not for sleep. [[/tesamorelin|Tesamorelin]] is sold as Egrifta, and its label is narrow: it “is indicated for the reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected adult patients with lipodystrophy.”[^egrifta] Lipodystrophy is an abnormal shift in body fat. Any other use, including sleep, is off-label. The label also says that “Long-term cardiovascular safety of EGRIFTA WR has not been established.”[^egrifta]

Then there is [[/emideltide|emideltide]], sold online as DSIP, short for delta sleep-inducing peptide. Its name makes a promise its record does not keep. FDA’s compounding advisory committee considered it in July 2026, and according to Healio’s report, “the votes on emideltide failed with 6 ‘yes’ votes, 7 ‘no’ votes and 1 abstaining.”[^healio] FDA has not posted an official vote record. FDA had already noted that it “has not identified safety-related information regarding emideltide for the proposed route of administration.”[^cat2] It is not part of the October 2026 HHS peptide policy.

The supplements in this lane are simpler. [[/glycine|Glycine]] is an amino acid sold as a dietary supplement; its only FDA approval as a drug is as a surgical irrigation fluid, which “is indicated for use as irrigating fluid during transurethral prostatic resection and other transurethral surgical procedures.”[^glycine] A 2026 scoping review found that “all 3 glycine sleep trials reported benefits on at least 1 sleep-related outcome,”[^fan] and added that “larger mechanistic trials with standardized sleep outcomes are needed.”[^fan] [[/magnesium|Magnesium]] has more trials but no clearer answer. A 2026 systematic review of 12 randomized trials found that “current evidence does not support oral magnesium as a routine treatment for insomnia.”[^mag] The reviewers rated the certainty of the evidence as low to very low.[^mag] [[/melatonin|Melatonin]] is sold as a supplement in the US, while the European Union has authorised prescription melatonin medicines for sleep.[^circadin]

For athletes, the growth hormone route is closed. The World Anti-Doping Agency’s list bans growth hormone-releasing factors, naming “growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) and its analogues (e.g. CJC-1293, CJC-1295, sermorelin and tesamorelin),”[^wada] along with the growth hormone secretagogues, at all times.[^wada] Glycine, magnesium and melatonin are not listed.

What is not known is whether any of the growth hormone drugs improves sleep in healthy men. No trial has tested sermorelin for sleep, the related peptides have little or no human sleep data, and the supplements’ trials are small. The one approved drug in the group, tesamorelin, was approved for something else entirely.
